lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use nodal stipule architecture and one-seeded angular fruit to distinguish Polygonaceae from other Caryophyllales.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first module with Polygonoideae ocrea door and Eriogonum-style involucre door
project_scope.note: The ocrea is characteristic of many Polygonaceae, especially Polygonoideae, but Eriogonum and other Eriogonoideae do not use the classic ocrea pattern.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Check the node for an ocrea: a papery or membranous sheath formed by stipular tissue around the stem. Then confirm a single-seeded 2- or 3-angled nut/achene and a persistent perianth.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Herbs, shrubs or vines; nodes often swollen. Leaves usually simple. Stipules are often fused into the nodal ocrea in Polygonoideae.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Small flowers with 2–6 tepals, often 5, commonly in spikes, racemes, panicles or clusters. Perianth persists and may enlarge, harden or become fleshy in fruit.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A one-seeded indehiscent nut/achene, commonly 2-sided or trigonous/3-angled.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Look at the node: an ocrea is a stipular tube ABOVE the leaf insertion, unlike a grass sheath. Eriogonum lacks this classic ocrea; identify its involucral cups by examining the separate flowers inside. Compare the persistent tepal envelope and one-seeded achene with Nyctaginaceae anthocarps, Amaranthaceae utricles, and Paronychia's one-seeded exception. In Rumex, three inner tepals enlarge into fruiting valves.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: node/ocrea → small tepal flower → angled one-seeded fruit → Eriogonum exception → genus doors
visual_lesson.intro: Polygonaceae has one of the best vegetative family clues in botany—the ocrea—but only if you also learn the major Eriogonum-style exception.

steps.title: 1 · Find the ocrea at the node
steps.look_for: A papery or membranous tube/sheath encircling the stem just above the leaf base.
steps.why_it_matters: For Persicaria, Polygonum and Rumex relatives, the ocrea can identify the family before flowers are fully examined.

steps.title: 2 · Follow the flower to a 2- or 3-angled nut
steps.look_for: A single dry seed-like fruit that is lens-shaped or distinctly 3-angled, enclosed or accompanied by the persistent perianth.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit architecture confirms the family when the ocrea is subtle or absent.

steps.title: 3 · Rumex door: enlarged inner tepals become valves
steps.look_for: Three inner tepals enlarge around the achene; one or more may develop a grainlike tubercle.
steps.why_it_matters: The fruiting perianth is the easiest genus-level doorway for docks and sorrels.

steps.title: 4 · Persicaria/Polygonum door: ocrea + small clustered flowers
steps.look_for: Strong nodal ocreae and small flowers in axillary clusters or terminal spikes/racemes.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the classic knotweed smart-search pattern.

steps.title: 5 · Eriogonum door: no classic ocrea
steps.look_for: Small flowers clustered inside little involucres, often on branched or umbel-like inflorescences; the classic nodal ocrea is absent.
steps.why_it_matters: Eriogonum is the family exception that prevents 'no ocrea = not Polygonaceae' mistakes.

comparisons.title: Polygonaceae vs Amaranthaceae
comparisons.rule: Polygonaceae commonly has an ocrea and a 2- or 3-angled one-seeded nut. Amaranthaceae lacks the ocrea and emphasizes tiny papery/bracteate flowers and utricles.

comparisons.title: Polygonaceae vs Caryophyllaceae
comparisons.rule: Caryophyllaceae usually has opposite leaves and no ocrea; flowers commonly have distinct sepals and petals and fruits are often many-seeded capsules.

comparisons.title: Polygonoideae vs Eriogonum
comparisons.rule: Persicaria/Polygonum/Rumex relatives: ocrea is a major clue. Eriogonum: involucral flower clusters and no classic ocrea.

comparisons.title: Eriogonum vs Mirabilis
comparisons.rule: Both can have flower-bearing involucres. Eriogonum contains separate flowers and produces an achene; Mirabilis has a perianth-derived anthocarp enclosing its one-seeded fruit. Involucre alone does not establish family.

visual_lesson.caveat: Do not make the ocrea universal across Polygonaceae. Eriogonoideae, including Eriogonum, follows a different vegetative/inflorescence pattern.
